newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala GDP grew 3.1 pct in 1996 - econ minister.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala GDP grew 3.1 pct in 1996 - econ minister.

text.p: Guatemala's economy grew 3.1 percent in 1996, Economy Minister Juan Mauricio Wurmser said on Thursday.
Wurmser said the result fell short of the government target of between four to five percent growth for the year.
The 3.1 percent growth rate is the lowest Guatemala has registered in the 1990s. Growth in 1995 was 4.5 percent.
"We have to admit that we didn't achieve the objective we established at the beginning of the year -- which was to reach growth between four to five percent," Wurmser said.
According to the minister, low international prices for coffee, Guatemala's principal export, had a lot to do with the economic "de-accelaration."

He said low coffee prices also meant that other Central American countries, which form Guatemala's principal export market, consumed less Guatemalan products because they had lower coffee income as well.

The revaluation of the Guatemalan Quetzal compared to major currencies towards the end of the year made Guatemalan products less competitive, especially so-called non-traditional exports -- anything other than coffee, sugar, bananas and beef, the minister said.
Wurmser said high prices of imported fossil fuels, and soy and other flours also harmed growth. And, he said, bank lending rates of over 20 percent inhibited investment.
There was good news in 1996, however, the minister said.
"We almost managed to balance the budget and did not produce a deficit," Wurmser said.
The balanced budget would help in 1997 as Guatemala works to pay off internal debt, mostly owed on short-term government bonds, he said.
The minister predicted stronger growth this year.
"The 1997 economy will surpass that of 1996. We are aiming again for growth over four percent," he said.
